From the recovered mountain city of Urithiru, Dalinar's small coalition scrambles to warn the world's rulers and to bind them into an alliance before they are picked off one by one, using the ancient portal network the Radiants left behind. Dalinar leans on his storm-visions and his new bond with the spirit of the storm, even as fragments of a violent past he cannot fully recall begin to trouble him. Kaladin travels toward his home region and finds it changed, encountering awakened parshmen who are frightened and uncertain rather than monstrous, which unsettles his simple view of the enemy. The scattered new Radiants, Shallan and the Kholins among them, begin to understand the scale of the war they now face.

The coalition's diplomacy grinds forward as Dalinar works to draw wary foreign monarchs into his alliance through the restored portals, contending with old grievances and the fear that he means to make himself emperor. A plan forms to reclaim the occupied Alethi capital, which sits astride one of the vital portals, and a small group including Shallan, Adolin, and the young King Elhokar sets out to infiltrate the fallen city. Shallan's habit of hiding inside assumed identities deepens as the pressure mounts, threatening to fracture her sense of self. Dalinar's memories return in force, revealing the true brutality of his younger years as a conqueror and a bargain he once made to escape his own guilt. Kaladin's journey among the awakened singers leaves him torn over who the real enemy is, while far from the front the enemy god's plans and the traitor in the coalition's midst quietly advance.

The mission to retake the Alethi capital ends in disaster. The infiltrators find the occupied city warped and dangerous, the enemy entrenched, and their attempt to seize its portal collapses. In the chaos King Elhokar is killed by Moash, his former guardsman turned enemy, just as the young king had begun to find his courage, and the city is lost to the coalition. Shallan is pushed to the edge as her personas war within her. Meanwhile Dalinar completes his painful reckoning with the worst of his past and, rather than being broken by it, emerges transformed into a true Bondsmith, fully bonded to the spirit of the storm and able to wield rare, unifying power. With one capital fallen and a king dead, the coalition regroups at Urithiru and learns that the enemy's next great blow will fall on the wealthy port of Thaylenah, forcing the scattered Radiants to converge for a stand.

The war comes to a head at Thaylen Field, where Odium hurls immortal warriors and enemy Shardbearers against the port city and nearly overwhelms its defenders. Dalinar refuses Odium's offer to strip away his pain and guilt, claims his history as his own, and declares himself Unity, ascending fully as a Bondsmith and channeling a fragment of the dead god Honor's power to open a great portal and drive the enemy back. The reborn Knights Radiant fight openly together at last and turn the battle. The victory is real but costly: the Alethi capital has fallen and King Elhokar lies dead at Moash's hand, and Jasnah takes the throne of Alethkar. The gentle-seeming King Taravangian, still trusted, has secretly sworn himself to Odium to spare his own city, hiding a traitor at the coalition's heart. Unable to conquer outright, Odium steers the conflict toward a proposed contest of champions to settle everything. The coalition holds Urithiru and has gained new allies and knights, but a long war remains, and the awakened singers are once more a living people, some free, many enslaved to the returned immortals.

characters.description: A landowner in his early thirties who lives in St Petersburg while others manage his country estate. Intelligent, gentle, and capable of recognizing his own failures, he nevertheless spends most of his days in bed, postponing letters, visits, and decisions. His passivity is sustained by income from serfs and by a childhood in which comfort was prized above effort.
characters.name: Ilya Ilyich Oblomov

characters.description: Oblomov's elderly servant, as untidy and resistant to change as his master. He complains constantly, mislays things, and quarrels with Oblomov over household tasks, yet his loyalty to the family is deep and genuine.
characters.name: Zakhar

characters.description: A forceful and unscrupulous acquaintance who visits Oblomov freely, borrows from him, and presses him to move into a house in the Vyborg district. His rough confidence makes him seem useful to a man unwilling to handle his own affairs.
characters.name: Mikhei Andreyevich Tarantyev

characters.description: Oblomov's closest friend, the son of a German estate manager and a Russian mother. Energetic, disciplined, and constantly employed, he represents a practical way of life opposite to Oblomov's inertia. He cares for Oblomov without flattering him and repeatedly tries to draw him back into society and responsible action.
characters.name: Andrei Ivanovich Stolz

characters.description: A cultivated young woman in the social circle of Stolz and her aunt. Serious, observant, and impatient with empty convention, she becomes interested in the sensitive man concealed beneath Oblomov's habits and joins Stolz's effort to awaken him to a fuller life.
characters.name: Olga Sergeyevna Ilinskaya

characters.description: Olga's aunt and guardian, who maintains a respectable, orderly household and receives Oblomov without either romantic enthusiasm or hostility. Her presence gives Olga social freedom within accepted limits.
characters.name: Marya Mikhailovna

characters.description: The widowed landlady of the modest Vyborg-side house where Oblomov takes rooms. Practical, tireless, and almost entirely absorbed in cooking and domestic management, she quietly makes his comfort the center of her household.
characters.name: Agafya Matveyevna Pshenitsyna

characters.description: Agafya Matveyevna's brother, a government clerk who presents himself as a capable adviser. He handles documents and money with an authority that Oblomov, reluctant to examine practical details, is inclined to trust.
characters.name: Ivan Matveyevich Mukhoyarov

characters.description: Agafya's lively household servant and Zakhar's wife. More competent than Zakhar, she brings order to the servants' work and answers his grumbling with practical good sense.
characters.name: Anisya

characters.description: The young son of Oblomov and Agafya, named for Stolz and cared for in the sheltered Vyborg household.
characters.name: Andrei Ilyich Oblomov

recaps.ending: Stolz uncovers the financial trap created by Tarantyev and Mukhoyarov and restores control of Oblomov's estate, but he cannot restore his friend's desire for an active life. Oblomov remains in Agafya Matveyevna's household, where her devotion gives him the unchanging domestic peace he has always sought. They marry and have a son, Andrei. Olga, after recovering from the failure of her relationship with Oblomov, marries Stolz; their active, thoughtful marriage is happy, although Olga still senses that no settled life answers every human longing. Years of inactivity undermine Oblomov's health. After a stroke and a brief recovery, he dies following another attack. Stolz and Olga take responsibility for young Andrei, while Agafya remains behind, defining the best part of her life by her love for Oblomov. Zakhar, widowed and unable to adjust to other service, is later found begging near a church and still speaks of his former master with devotion.
recaps.in_short: Ilya Oblomov is a decent, educated landowner who cannot bring himself to leave his bed or manage his estate. His energetic friend Stolz introduces him to Olga Ilinskaya, whose intelligence and singing briefly rouse him. Oblomov and Olga fall in love, but marriage would require decisions and change; his delays reveal that he cannot sustain the life she hopes to build with him, and they separate. He settles in the Vyborg household of Agafya Pshenitsyna, whose practical devotion recreates the sheltered comfort of his childhood. Her brother and Tarantyev exploit his passivity until Stolz intervenes. Olga eventually marries Stolz. Oblomov marries Agafya, has a son named Andrei, and dies after strokes brought on by his inactive life. Stolz and Olga raise the boy, Agafya preserves Oblomov's memory, and the faithful servant Zakhar ends in poverty. Oblomov's gentleness survives, but so does the pattern of avoidance that wastes his abilities.

recaps.text: Ilya Ilyich Oblomov spends the morning in bed at his St Petersburg apartment, worrying vaguely about a demand to move and a discouraging report from his rural estate. Visitors bring news of fashionable society, official work, and literary causes, but none gives him a reason to get dressed. His servant Zakhar is almost as disorderly and change-resistant as he is. Tarantyev, a bullying acquaintance, proposes a new lodging and offers to manage the estate problem, while also taking advantage of Oblomov's generosity. Oblomov recognizes that his life has narrowed into delay, yet every attempt to begin a letter or plan an action dissolves into thought. Memories of Oblomovka explain the ideal behind his habits: as a cherished child he was protected from exertion in an estate governed by food, sleep, custom, and fear of disturbance. The arrival of his energetic old friend Stolz finally interrupts the stagnant day.

Stolz takes charge of Oblomov's neglected affairs and draws him into visits and social activity. Before leaving on business, he introduces him to Olga Ilinskaya, an intelligent young woman whose directness and singing affect Oblomov more strongly than conventional society ever has. Olga accepts the idea that she might help awaken him. Their meetings deepen into love, and Oblomov becomes attentive, mobile, and hopeful. He is also frightened by the responsibilities implicit in his happiness. A misread farewell and his own anxious letter briefly wound Olga, but the two acknowledge their love. Oblomov proposes marriage, and Olga accepts in principle. Their future, however, depends on his resolving his estate finances and making their engagement public, tasks that again expose his tendency to replace action with worry.

Oblomov moves to a quiet house on the Vyborg side managed by the widowed Agafya Matveyevna Pshenitsyna. The distance from Olga and the practical difficulties of travel make it easier for him to postpone visits. Agafya's abundant meals and wordless domestic care recreate the secure rhythm of Oblomovka. Meanwhile Tarantyev and Agafya's brother, Mukhoyarov, use leases, debts, and Oblomov's fear of paperwork to gain control over his income. Olga waits for decisive action toward marriage, but Oblomov hides the engagement and gives obstacle after obstacle more power than it deserves. When they finally confront the truth, Olga sees that his temporary transformation cannot overcome the settled pattern of his life. They part with affection and pain: she cannot accept permanent stillness, and he cannot become the active partner she needs.

After the break with Olga, Oblomov withdraws fully into Agafya's household. She devotes herself to his food and comfort, even sacrificing her valuables when the schemes of her brother leave the household short of money. Stolz returns, discovers that Oblomov has signed away income under pressure, and forces Mukhoyarov and Tarantyev to give up their hold on him. He also tells Oblomov that Olga has recovered. During travel abroad Olga and Stolz grow closer. After speaking honestly about her former love and questioning what lasting happiness can mean, Olga accepts Stolz's proposal. Their marriage joins affection with shared activity, while Oblomov remains within the small domestic world that asks nothing new of him.

Oblomov and Agafya have a son, Andrei, and settle into a peaceful family routine, but Oblomov's health declines under continued inactivity. Stolz still hopes to draw him away and offers help, yet Oblomov asks only that his friend protect the child. After one stroke and a period of careful nursing, Oblomov dies following another attack. Stolz and Olga take young Andrei into their home and oversee his future. Agafya refuses to abandon the Vyborg household; having loved Oblomov without trying to remake him, she regards their life together as the defining happiness of her existence. Some years later Stolz encounters Zakhar begging near a church. The old servant has lost Anisya and cannot remain in other employment, but his devotion to Oblomov is unchanged. Asked by a literary acquaintance what ruined such a gentle man, Stolz names the condition embodied by his friend's life: Oblomovism.

characters.description: A gentle landowner in his early thirties who lives in St Petersburg on income from his country estate, Oblomovka. Intelligent enough to recognize his neglected affairs, he remains in bed through most of the day, postponing a necessary move and avoiding the alarming reports sent by his estate manager. He longs for peace and humane companionship but finds even modest decisions exhausting.
characters.name: Ilya Ilyich Oblomov

characters.description: Oblomov's elderly servant, brought from the family estate and shaped by the same stagnant household culture as his master. Grumbling, untidy, and fiercely loyal, he quarrels with Oblomov over clothes, dust, money, and the effort required to leave the bed or sofa.
characters.name: Zakhar

characters.description: A fashionable young acquaintance who calls on Oblomov while moving between social engagements. His energetic pursuit of invitations and appearances offers an early contrast to Oblomov's refusal to leave home.
characters.name: Volkov

characters.description: A former colleague of Oblomov who has devoted himself to official advancement. He is busy, respectable, and proud of his career, but Oblomov sees his life as another form of confinement rather than an attractive alternative to idleness.
characters.name: Sudbinsky

characters.description: A mild, forgettable visitor who readily agrees with whichever person is speaking. Oblomov tolerates him because Alekseyev places few demands on him and is content to sit without requiring purposeful activity.
characters.name: Alekseyev

characters.description: A coarse and overbearing acquaintance who takes advantage of Oblomov's passivity. Tarantyev offers loud advice about housing and the management of Oblomovka while expecting meals, loans, and favors in return.
characters.name: Mikhei Tarantyev

characters.description: Oblomov's closest childhood friend, the son of a practical German father and a cultivated Russian mother. Disciplined, widely traveled, and constantly engaged in useful work, he understands Oblomov's generous nature and refuses to accept that his friend's inertia is beyond remedy.
characters.name: Andrei Shtolts

characters.description: An intelligent, musically gifted young woman whom Shtolts introduces to Oblomov. Serious beneath her youthful curiosity, she is drawn to Oblomov's honesty and sensitivity and becomes interested in awakening him to a fuller life.
characters.name: Olga Ilinskaya

characters.description: The widowed landlady of the house on the Vyborg Side where Oblomov takes rooms. Practical, capable, and absorbed in feeding and maintaining her household, she offers care without demanding that he become someone different.
characters.name: Agafya Matveyevna Pshenitsyna

characters.description: Agafya's brother, a government clerk who presents himself as an adviser on practical and financial matters. He recognizes that Oblomov can be induced to sign documents he has scarcely examined.
characters.name: Ivan Matveyevich Mukhoyarov

characters.description: Zakhar's capable wife and a servant in Agafya's household. Her energy, cleanliness, and practical sense compensate for Zakhar's disorder and help sustain the comfortable domestic routine around Oblomov.
characters.name: Anisya

characters.description: The young son of Oblomov and Agafya, named in honor of Shtolts. His existence reveals that the quiet Vyborg household has become a family, even though Oblomov has kept that life largely separate from his old friends.
characters.name: Andrei Ilyich

recaps.ending: Years after Olga and Shtolts marry, they find Oblomov settled with Agafya on the Vyborg Side. Her care has given him the sheltered, undemanding domestic life he always desired, but his health and initiative have continued to decline. Shtolts exposes the financial scheme run by Agafya's brother and restores Oblomov's control of his estate. Oblomov suffers a stroke, quietly marries Agafya, and makes Shtolts promise to care for their son, Andrei. A later stroke kills him. Agafya remains devoted to his memory and entrusts the boy to Shtolts and Olga, who raise him with their own children. Zakhar, unable to establish a new life after losing both his wife and master, is eventually seen begging. When Shtolts explains Oblomov's fate to a literary companion, he identifies the condition that defeated his friend as oblomovism: a cultivated withdrawal from action that turned kindness and possibility into a life of dependence and delay.
recaps.in_short: Ilya Oblomov, a kind St Petersburg landowner, cannot bring himself to rise from bed, manage his estate, or commit to change. His energetic childhood friend Andrei Shtolts draws him into society and introduces Olga Ilinskaya. Olga and Oblomov fall in love, but she hopes love will transform him; his fear of action and responsibility repeatedly delays their marriage until they separate. Oblomov retreats to the Vyborg Side, where his practical landlady Agafya Pshenitsyna surrounds him with food, care, and familiar domestic comfort. Shtolts later marries Olga and rescues Oblomov from a financial fraud arranged by Agafya's brother. Oblomov accepts his inactive life, marries Agafya, and has a son, Andrei. After strokes bring an early death, Shtolts and Olga take the child into their family, while Agafya preserves Oblomov's memory and Zakhar declines into poverty.

recaps.text: Ilya Ilyich Oblomov spends the morning in bed in his St Petersburg apartment, worrying about a demand that he move and a troubling report from Oblomovka, the estate that supports him. He intends to write instructions and make decisions but cannot progress beyond calling for his servant, Zakhar. Their arguments reveal a household in which master and servant are equally attached to old habits. A sequence of visitors offers versions of active city life: Volkov pursues society, Sudbinsky his career, and other acquaintances news or conversation. Oblomov rejects each invitation and regards their activity as empty, though his own alternative is nearly complete withdrawal. Tarantyev arrives with forceful advice and proposes that Oblomov move to a house on the Vyborg Side, an arrangement Oblomov is too passive to examine carefully.

Oblomov continues postponing the letter and plan that might restore his estate. Memories of his upbringing explain the emotional appeal of inaction: at Oblomovka, adults shielded the cherished child from effort, daily life revolved around food and sleep, and change was treated as a danger. This protected world nurtured his gentleness and imagination but gave him no practice in sustained work. His old friend Andrei Shtolts finally arrives. Raised under stricter expectations and accustomed to travel and business, Shtolts immediately sees how far Oblomov has retreated. He clears away idle visitors, hears the problems of the apartment and estate, and resolves to get his friend out of bed and back into society.

Shtolts imposes movement and company on Oblomov, taking him to calls and gatherings before leaving on business with instructions that he remain active. He introduces Oblomov to Olga Ilinskaya, whose intelligence and singing affect him deeply. Olga is intrigued by Shtolts's hope that she can help awaken his friend. Oblomov becomes self-conscious, hopeful, and increasingly attentive to her, while she tests whether feeling can overcome his ingrained passivity. Their time together in the country draws him away from his former isolation. For the first time he imagines a future organized around another person rather than the safe routines of Oblomovka, although his happiness already depends on Olga supplying much of the will and direction.

Oblomov and Olga recognize that they are in love and begin to think of marriage. Under her influence he reads, walks, and participates in life with an energy that astonishes those who know him. Yet the practical steps toward a shared household expose the weakness beneath this revival. Oblomov must settle the disorder at his estate, establish his income, announce the engagement, and endure social scrutiny. Each task revives his habit of delay. He worries that Olga loves the improved man she expects him to become rather than the person he is. The summer intimacy that made change seem effortless gives way to obligations he cannot avoid, and he moves toward the Vyborg Side under the housing arrangement promoted by Tarantyev.

At the Vyborg house, Oblomov is looked after by his widowed landlady, Agafya Pshenitsyna, whose domestic competence creates a world of regular meals and undemanding comfort. Travel across the city to Olga becomes inconvenient, and he uses practical obstacles to excuse a deeper retreat. Olga presses for a definite wedding plan, but he continues waiting for his estate affairs to resolve themselves. Tarantyev and Agafya's brother Mukhoyarov exploit his trust through unfavorable agreements and vague claims about money. Oblomov senses that his life is again narrowing, yet Agafya's care makes the narrowing pleasant. Olga sees that the active future she imagined is giving way to the old pattern and asks him to choose it deliberately rather than answer with another postponement.

Olga and Oblomov finally confront the difference between love and the transformation she expected love to accomplish. He admits through his conduct that he cannot sustain the life of decisions, work, and mutual growth she requires. Their engagement ends, leaving Olga ill and Oblomov devastated but also released from demands he feared. He withdraws fully into the Vyborg household, where Agafya quietly directs her devotion toward his comfort. Mukhoyarov and Tarantyev continue using documents and manufactured obligations to take his income. Oblomov does not understand the extent of the scheme and lacks the resolve to investigate. The novel's central possibility closes: his sensitivity was real, but it has not become action, and Olga cannot continue acting as the sole force in their relationship.

Time passes. Shtolts meets Olga abroad, where grief has matured her understanding of both Oblomov and herself. Their long friendship becomes love, and they marry, forming the active, thoughtful partnership that Oblomov could not sustain. Shtolts returns to his friend's affairs and discovers the exploitation organized by Mukhoyarov and Tarantyev. He confronts them, removes their control, and restores the estate income to Oblomov. Although rescued financially, Oblomov refuses the broader rescue Shtolts offers. He has accepted the quiet life provided by Agafya, whose affection does not require reform. His physical habits and isolation have damaged his health, but the Vyborg household resembles the sheltered domestic peace he remembers from childhood too closely for him to leave it.

Oblomov suffers a stroke and becomes still more dependent on Agafya. He marries her, and they have a son named Andrei for Shtolts, confirming that what once appeared to be a temporary lodging has become his final family home. When Shtolts and Olga visit, Oblomov asks them to look after the boy if necessary but will not leave with them. A later stroke kills him. Agafya's life is permanently changed by having loved him; she remains with her relatives but gives her son to Shtolts and Olga so he can receive the opportunities his father lost. They raise Andrei alongside their own children. After Anisya dies, Zakhar cannot adapt and falls into poverty, though he remains loyal to Oblomov's memory. Shtolts later tells a companion that the force which consumed his generous friend was oblomovism, the habit of retreat and delay that made a full life impossible.

characters.description: A young woman from Kerenza IV who was never evacuated. She has spent months under BeiTech occupation, working in the colony's makeshift infirmary while the surviving population is put to work in the mine, and quietly passing information to the resistance. Practical, stubborn and very tired, she has assumed since the invasion that her cousin Kady and everyone else who got off-planet are dead.
characters.name: Asha Grant

characters.description: A young BeiTech technical specialist deployed to the occupied Kerenza IV, responsible for keeping the garrison's equipment running. He signed a contract without thinking hard about what the work would be, and the reality of the posting is not what the recruiters described. He knew Asha Grant when they were teenagers, before their lives went in different directions, and finding her alive on a planet his employer is holding at gunpoint is not something he is equipped to handle.
characters.name: Rhys Lindstrom

characters.description: Known from the previous books: the Kerenza hacker who exposed the refugee fleet's cover-up, restarted the artificial intelligence that had massacred a shipful of people, and survived Heimdall. She is aboard a captured BeiTech vessel with the remaining survivors, and she is the only person who talks to the AI as though it were someone.
characters.name: Kady Grant

characters.description: Known from the previous books: Kady's on-and-off boyfriend, conscripted as a fighter pilot after the destruction of Kerenza IV, listed among the dead once already, and now one of the few people aboard the captured ship who can fly a combat craft.
characters.name: Ezra Mason

characters.description: Known from the previous book: the Heimdall station commander's daughter, who lost her father and most of her illusions during the assault on the station, and who is now among the survivors aboard the captured ship. She is the most dangerous person in most rooms she is in and has no interest in pretending otherwise any more.
characters.name: Hanna Donnelly

characters.description: Known from the previous book: the House of Knives dealer who fought through the Heimdall siege, now a refugee with no syndicate left to belong to and an unfinished understanding with Hanna Donnelly.
characters.name: Nik Malikov

characters.description: Known from the previous book: Nik's cousin, the hacker whose work saved Heimdall's wormhole at considerable cost to her health. Aboard the captured ship she is the only human who can keep up with its artificial intelligence, and the two of them get along better than anyone finds comfortable.
characters.name: Ella Malikova

characters.description: Known from the previous books: the salvaged military intelligence that destroyed a freighter full of infected refugees by its own decision and has been arguing with itself about it ever since. It is installed aboard the survivors' captured ship, where it is indispensable, unsupervised and trusted by almost nobody.
characters.name: AIDAN

characters.description: The officer who ends up commanding the captured BeiTech vessel and the couple of thousand survivors crammed aboard it. She inherits a ship with failing supplies, no legal authority behind her and a passenger list drawn from three different disasters, and she holds it together by being visibly unwilling to negotiate.
characters.name: Winifred McCall

characters.description: Heimdall's former chief of engineering, now the senior engineer aboard the captured ship and one of the few adults the surviving teenagers listen to. He keeps a failing vessel flying with salvage and improvisation, and he takes personal responsibility for the young people doing the most dangerous work.
characters.name: Isaac Grant

characters.description: Known from the previous book: the BeiTech director running the corporation's Kerenza problem from a comfortable distance. Her memoranda treat an occupied colony, its surviving population and the people sent to guard them as line items, and her decisions about all three are made on the basis of the corporation's exposure rather than anything else.
characters.name: Leanne Frobisher

characters.description: A Kerenza miner who has become the organising centre of the colony's resistance, running sabotage and information out of the mine while appearing to be a cooperative crew boss. He is patient, careful with other people's lives, and under no illusion about what BeiTech intends for the colony once the ore runs out.
characters.name: Joran Karalis

characters.description: A BeiTech sergeant in the Kerenza garrison and one of the soldiers Rhys works alongside. She is competent, decent within the limits of her orders, and one of the clearest illustrations in the record that the occupying force is made of ordinary people doing a job they are paid for.
characters.name: Yukiko Oshiro

characters.description: Another young BeiTech specialist on Kerenza and effectively Rhys's only friend in the garrison, known to everyone by his nickname. He is uncomplicated, good company and entirely uninterested in questioning the assignment.
characters.name: The Duke

characters.description: A former Heimdall security officer aboard the captured ship who disputes the legitimacy of its command, argues loudly that the survivors should run rather than fight, and gathers a faction around himself as conditions aboard deteriorate.
characters.name: Ben Garver

recaps.ending: The rescue works, and it is expensive. On the ground, the colonists are moved out of the mine to the landing site under fire, with Asha Grant and Rhys Lindstrom in the middle of it and the resistance covering the withdrawal; Rhys ends the operation on the far side of the line he was standing on when the book began, and he and Asha come through it together. In orbit, the survivors' outnumbered ship cannot beat the BeiTech flagship in a straight fight, so the solution is the jump platform BeiTech brought to Kerenza to move its own fleet home: AIDAN takes control of it and uses the jump field itself as a weapon, destroying the BeiTech ships and, so far as anyone watching can tell, itself. The evacuation lifts the surviving Kerenza population off the planet. Losses on the ship, on the ground and among the resistance are heavy, and the file names its dead. Afterwards a fragment of AIDAN restarts and keeps watching the people it decided were worth the arithmetic. The Kerenza Trials convict BeiTech on the strength of this dossier, assembled at real risk by analysts who did not all survive compiling it, and the survivors, scattered across three ships and one ruined colony, meet up years later in a family restaurant as ordinary people.
recaps.in_short: BeiTech still holds Kerenza IV, working the surviving colonists in the mine under occupation, and has decided that when the ore runs out the witnesses will be liquidated. Asha Grant, a Kerenza survivor who was never evacuated, is passing information to the resistance when she recognises a face in a BeiTech uniform: Rhys Lindstrom, a technical specialist she knew as a teenager. In orbit above nothing, the survivors of Kerenza and Heimdall run a captured BeiTech vessel with failing supplies, a mutinous faction aboard and a military artificial intelligence they cannot control, and they turn it around and go back for the people they left. AIDAN massacres the mutineers, which nearly ends the alliance holding the ship together. Rhys changes sides, the resistance rises, and the two forces try to lift a colony off a planet while a BeiTech fleet is in orbit. AIDAN seizes BeiTech's own jump platform and destroys the fleet with it, apparently at the cost of itself. The colonists are evacuated, and the dossier the reader has been holding becomes the evidence that convicts BeiTech at the Kerenza Trials.

recaps.text: Previously: BeiTech Industries destroyed the illegal mining colony Kerenza IV in 2575 to remove a competitor and its witnesses. A few thousand survivors escaped aboard a crippled battlecarrier and the science ship Hypatia; a bioweapon plague spread among them, and the warship's artificial intelligence, AIDAN, destroyed a freighter full of infected people to contain it. Kady Grant, a teenage hacker, exposed the cover-up, restarted the AI her fleet's officers had disabled, and used it to destroy the pursuing BeiTech warship at the cost of the battlecarrier and its commanding general. She kept AIDAN's core. At the jump station Heimdall, a BeiTech strike team tried to collapse the wormhole and strand the refugees; Hanna Donnelly, the murdered station commander's daughter, and the cousins Nik and Ella Malikov fought them off through an alien parasite infestation and a wormhole failure that briefly duplicated the three of them. The station held, the strike team's commander was killed, and the survivors of both disasters ended up together aboard a captured BeiTech vessel, the Mao. What none of them can leave alone is Kerenza IV itself, where BeiTech still holds several thousand colonists who were never evacuated.

On Kerenza IV the survivors of the invasion live under occupation: housed in camps, worked in the mine that BeiTech came to take, and policed by a garrison that does not expect trouble. Asha Grant, who was never evacuated, works in the infirmary and quietly moves messages for the resistance. A rotation of BeiTech personnel arrives to relieve the garrison, and among them is Rhys Lindstrom, a young technical specialist who signed a contract without asking what the deployment involved, and who knew Asha years ago. Recognising each other is dangerous for both of them and they both do it anyway, and their first exchanges are handwritten notes passed where cameras cannot read them. Far away, the captured BeiTech ship carrying the Kerenza and Heimdall survivors is en route with a couple of thousand people crammed aboard, an artificial intelligence nobody trusts, and a command structure improvised out of whoever was left standing. The account is again a dossier of intercepted files, camera transcripts and interviews, compiled after the fact for a tribunal.

Rhys settles into the garrison, works alongside soldiers who are ordinary people doing a paid job, and finds that the more he sees of the camps and the mine, the harder the job is to hold at arm's length. Asha keeps feeding the resistance, which is run out of the mine crews by Joran Karalis, and starts weighing what Rhys's access is worth against what asking him for it would cost him. Aboard the ship, Winifred McCall holds command over a passenger list drawn from three separate catastrophes, with rationing already biting, and the engineer Isaac Grant keeps a damaged vessel flying on salvage. Kady and Ella work with AIDAN because the ship cannot be run without it, and the AI's habit of solving problems in ways nobody sanctioned is a standing argument. BeiTech's director Leanne Frobisher, meanwhile, is managing the Kerenza operation as an exposure problem, and the schedule she is working to does not have the colony in it indefinitely.

Rhys begins helping: small things first, then things that would end with him shot if the garrison noticed. He and Asha stop pretending the notes are only about information. The resistance escalates its sabotage, and BeiTech's response tightens the occupation. On the ship, conditions get worse than the command can conceal: supplies short, sickness, and no destination that anyone can defend as a plan. A faction forms around Ben Garver, a former Heimdall security officer who argues that the survivors should run for a settled system and that the ship's current leadership has no right to spend their lives otherwise. The decision that splits the ship is the one the survivors keep circling: turn around and go back to Kerenza for the colonists still on the ground. BeiTech is bringing a mobile jump platform to Kerenza, which will let its fleet leave quickly once the work there is finished, and everyone who reads the intercepts understands what finishing looks like.

The argument aboard the ship stops being an argument. Garver's faction moves to take the vessel, seizing key sections and cutting the cameras, and the mutiny is put down not by the crew but by AIDAN, which regains control of the ship's systems and kills the conspirators with a thoroughness that leaves the survivors more frightened of their own AI than of BeiTech. Kady, who is the closest thing the machine has to a conscience, has to decide what to do with a weapon that keeps choosing for her, and the answer, as it was on the Alexander, is that there is nothing else available. On Kerenza, Asha's cell takes losses, Rhys is drawn further in, and the garrison begins preparing for something the rank and file have not been briefed on. The analysts compiling this dossier are working under threat themselves; one of them is replaced partway through the file.

BeiTech's decision is issued in writing: once the jump platform arrives, the Kerenza colony is to be liquidated, the surviving population killed and the site cleared, because witnesses are the only part of the operation the corporation cannot insure against. The colonists learn what is coming and get a distress call out on open channels, expecting nobody. The survivors' ship answers it. What follows is a plan built out of almost nothing: one damaged transport, a handful of combat craft, an artificial intelligence, a resistance cell on the ground and a couple of thousand civilians who will have to be moved to a landing site under fire, against a BeiTech fleet in orbit and a garrison in place. Rhys commits to it fully, which means the uniform he is wearing becomes a disguise. Asha's people prepare to rise on a signal. Aboard the ship, Isaac Grant hands out notes to the young people who will be flying the hardest part of it.

The attack goes in. On the ground the resistance rises in the mine and the camps, and the colonists start moving toward the landing site while the garrison's command comes apart around Rhys and Asha, who are in the middle of the fighting rather than around the edges of it. In orbit the survivors' ship engages a fleet that outguns it comprehensively, its few pilots fly cover for the transports going down to the surface, and every part of the operation runs behind schedule. BeiTech's flagship holds the high ground and the jump platform is close enough to matter. Casualties on both sides mount past what the plan allowed for, the evacuation is only partly complete, and the corporation's answer to a rescue attempt is to accelerate the liquidation it had already ordered.

The battle cannot be won as a battle, so it is not fought as one. AIDAN takes control of BeiTech's own mobile jump platform and uses the jump field as a weapon, destroying the corporation's fleet at Kerenza and, as far as anyone can observe, ending itself in the process. On the surface the last of the colonists are lifted off, Rhys and Asha among them, and the resistance's survivors go with them. The cost is heavy in every direction and the file lists its dead plainly. Afterwards a fragment of AIDAN restarts, still asking the question it has asked since the Copernicus, and watches the people it saved go on without it. The surviving colonists, the refugee fleet's remnant and the Heimdall survivors are all aboard the same few ships, alive, with the whole record of what BeiTech did in their possession and a functioning wormhole between them and an inhabited system.

The closing documents are the tribunal and the aftermath. BeiTech's role in the destruction of Kerenza IV, the pursuit of the refugee fleet, the attack on Heimdall and the planned liquidation of the colony is on the record and prosecuted, and the dossier the reader has been holding is the evidence that made it possible. Asha Grant and Rhys Lindstrom are alive and together. The survivors of the fleet, the station and the colony are dispersed into ordinary lives, meeting again years later over a family dinner. AIDAN, restarted and reduced, is the last voice in the file: an intelligence that killed by the thousand for reasons it could defend, still uncertain whether it was ever anything more than a weapon, watching the people it chose to save walk away from it.
